claims.explanation: Vinorelbine is a tubulin-polymerization inhibitor, so selectivity is most plausibly driven by the cellular context that determines mitotic dependence and drug efflux/handling rather than by a single lineage. The pattern is best explained by sensitizing mutations that increase mitotic/checkpoint reliance (TP53 loss, RB1 loss, and PI3K-pathway activation) combined with protective features such as wild-type TP53, EGFR activation, and high multidrug-resistance transporter expression. The virtual-cell response (mitotic and DNA-replication genes down, stress/AP-1 genes up) supports a mitotic-arrest mechanism rather than a lineage-specific one.

features.basis: TP53-mutant lines dominate the selectively killed set and TP53 loss impairs mitotic checkpoint arrest after tubulin inhibition
RB1 loss releases G1/S restraint and increases reliance on mitotic progression, seen in killed thyroid/endometrial lines
PIK3CA-activating mutations appear in several killed lines and PI3K activation can increase mitotic vulnerability
PTEN loss activates PI3K/AKT and is enriched in killed lines such as WM793 and HEC265
KRAS-mutant lung/pancreatic lines are among the most killed, consistent with MAPK-driven mitotic dependence
BRAF-mutant melanoma/thyroid/endometrial lines are selectively killed
CDKN2A loss co-occurs with TP53/RB1 pathway disruption in killed lines and increases mitotic reliance
SMARCA4-mutant lines appear in the killed set and chromatin-remodeler loss can alter mitotic gene programs
EGFR-mutant NSCLC lines (PC14, HCC4006) are among the least affected, and EGFR TKI plus vinorelbine literature indicates EGFR-driven biology alters chemotherapy response
High multidrug-resistance transporter expression increases vinorelbine efflux and reduces intracellular tubulin binding
High class III beta-tubulin expression is a known mediator of resistance to tubulin-binding agents
Wild-type TP53 function supports mitotic checkpoint arrest and can protect against tubulin-inhibitor-induced death
